source_text: Καὶ δῆτα δικαίους μὲν καὶ φρονίμους καὶ σώφρονας, ἢ ἀνδρείους ἡμᾶς ὑπὸ ἡμετέρας βραδυτῆτος καὶ νωχελίας, καὶ ταῦτα πάνυ σπεύδων, ἔτι μέλλει καταστήσασθαι, οὔτε ἔχοντας, οὔτε ἐγγύς που γενομένους οὐδ' ἡστινοσοῦν ἀρετῆς ἀνθρώπων ἢ θείας, πολλοῦ γε δεῖ. αὗται γὰρ μέγισται ὑψηλαί, καὶ οὐδ' ἑτέρα ληπτέα, οὐδὲ τῷ τυχεῖν, ὅτῳ μὴ Θεός γε ἐμπνέοι δύναμιν· ἡμεῖς τε οὔτε πεφύκαμεν οὕτως ἐπιτηδείως, οὔτε καὶ ἄξιοι εἶναι ἐπιτυχεῖν οὐδέπω ὁμολογοῦμεν· οὐ ποιήσαντες ἀπὸ ῥᾳθυμίας καὶ ἀσθενείας πάντα, ἅπερ τοὺς τῶν ἀρίστων ἐφιεμένους, καὶ τὰ τέλεια μνωμένους χρή. δίκαιοι μὲν οὖν ἢ σώφρονες, ἤ τινα τῶν ἄλλων ἔχειν ἀρετῶν, ἔτι μέλλομεν· ἐραστὰς δὲ ἡμᾶς ὅτι δριμύτατον ἐρῶντας ἔρωτα, ὅσπερ ἐπ' αὐτῷ μόνον ἴσως, καὶ πάλαι κατεστήσατο ὁ θαυμαστὸς οὗτος, καὶ φίλος τῶν ἀρετῶν, καὶ προήγορος· ἐμποιήσας ἔρωτα τῇ αὐτοῦ ἀρετῇ, καὶ τοῦ κάλλους τῆς δικαιοσύνης, ἧς τὸ χρύσεον ὄντως ἔδειξεν ἡμῖν πρόσωπον, καὶ φρονήσεως τῆς πᾶσιν ἐφεσίμου, καὶ τῆς ἐρασμιωτάτης σοφίας τῆς ἀληθοῦς, καὶ σωφροσύνης τῆς θεοειδοῦς, ἥ ἐστι ψυχῆς εὐστάθεια καὶ εἰρήνη πᾶσι τοῖς κτησαμένοις αὐτήν, καὶ ἀνδρείας τῆς θαυμασιωτάτης ὑπομονῆς, καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν εὐσεβείας, ἣν μητέρα φασὶ τῶν ἀρετῶν, ὀρθῶς λέγοντες. αὕτη γάρ ἐστιν ἀρχὴ καὶ τελευτὴ πασῶν τῶν ἀρετῶν· ἀπὸ ταύτης τε γὰρ ὁρμωμένοις, ῥᾷστα ἂν ἡμῖν ἐπιγένοιντο καὶ αἱ λοιπαὶ ἀρεταί· εἰ τοῦθ' ὃ δὴ πάντα ἄνθρωπον, τόν γε μὴ ἄθεον ἢ φιλήδονον, τὸ φίλον γενέσθαι καὶ προσήγορον Θεῷ, κτήσασθαι ἑαυτοῖς ἐπιθυμοῦντες καὶ σπεύδοντες, τῶν λοιπῶν ἀρετῶν ἐπιμελοίμεθα· ὅπως μὴ ἀνάξιοι καὶ ῥυπῶντες, μετὰ δὲ πάσης ἀρετῆς καὶ σοφίας, ὥσπερ τινὸς ἀγαθοῦ πομποῦ καὶ ἱερέως σοφωτάτου, προσίοιμεν τῷ Θεῷ. τό γε πάντων τέλος οὐχ ἕτερόν τι οἶμαι, ἢ καθαρῷ τῷ νῷ ἐξομοιωθέντα προσελθεῖν τῷ Θεῷ, καὶ μένειν ἐν αὐτῷ.
thought_title: Not yet virtuous, but made lovers of virtue
orientation: Gregory admits he has not yet gained the virtues, but Origen has made him a lover of them, whose goal is to draw near to God.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed just and prudent and self-controlled, or courageous, he is still about to establish us, by our slowness and sluggishness, and this though greatly hastening; [us] neither having nor having come anywhere near any virtue whatever, of men or divine — far from it. For these are greatest, lofty, and neither one is to be taken, nor by chance-getting, by one into whom God does not breathe power; and we neither are by nature so suited, nor do we yet confess to be worthy to attain; not having done, from laziness and weakness, all things which those aiming at the best and wooing the perfect must. Just then or self-controlled, or to have any of the other virtues, we are still about to be; but lovers us, loving with the sharpest love, which perhaps alone was in his power, this wonderful man, both friend and advocate of the virtues, established long ago; having instilled love by his own virtue, both of the beauty of justice, whose truly golden face he showed us, and of prudence desirable to all, and of the most lovely true wisdom, and of godlike self-control, which is steadiness and peace of soul to all who acquire it, and of courage, the most wonderful endurance, and above all of piety, which they call the mother of the virtues, saying rightly. For this is beginning and end of all the virtues; for to those setting out from it most easily would the remaining virtues also come upon us; if, desiring and hastening to acquire for ourselves this which every man — at least the one not godless or pleasure-loving — [must], to become friend and one addressing God, we should take care of the remaining virtues; so that not unworthy and filthy, but with all virtue and wisdom, as with some good escort and most wise priest, we might approach God. The end of all, I think, is nothing other than, having been made like by the pure mind, to come to God and to remain in Him.

pass_b_english: And indeed, because of our slowness and sluggishness, he has yet to make us just and prudent, self-controlled or courageous, earnestly as he strives for it. We neither have nor have come anywhere near any virtue at all, human or divine; far from it. For these are the greatest, the lofty virtues, and neither kind can be grasped, nor gained by chance, by anyone into whom God does not breathe power. We are not so well suited to them by nature, nor do we yet profess to be worthy to attain them, since through laziness and weakness we have not done all that those must do who aim at the best and seek after perfection. So we have yet to become just or self-controlled, or to have any of the other virtues. But lovers we are, loving with the keenest love; that, perhaps, was all that lay in his power, and this wonderful man, the friend and advocate of the virtues, made us such long ago. By his own virtue he kindled in us a love of the beauty of justice, whose truly golden face he showed us; of prudence, which all desire; of true wisdom, most lovely; of godlike self-control, which is steadiness and peace of soul for all who gain it; of courage, that most wonderful endurance; and above all of piety, which people rightly call the mother of the virtues. For piety is the beginning and the end of all the virtues. Starting from it, the other virtues too would come to us most easily, if we cared for the rest of them out of desire and eagerness to win for ourselves what every person must, at least every person who is not godless or a lover of pleasure: to become a friend of God and on familiar terms with Him. We would tend those virtues so that we might draw near to God not unworthy and soiled, but with every virtue and with wisdom as our good escort and most wise priest. And the goal of it all, I think, is nothing else than this: to draw near to God, made like Him by a pure mind, and to abide in Him.
notes: Copy-text: Greek column of the 1622 Paris Opera omnia (printed pp. 68-69), as in the source row. καταστήσασθαι (print; A corrected to -εσθαι): the sense, ‘has yet to make us’, is the same. μέγισται ὑψηλαί (print, no καί) rendered ‘the greatest, the lofty virtues’. οὐδ' ἑτέρα ληπτέα (print; A οὐδετέρα) taken as ‘neither kind’ (human or divine). οὐδὲ τῷ τυχεῖν (print = Vossius) rendered ‘nor gained by chance’; A’s οὐδέ τῳ would give ‘not by anyone’, with the same result. ὁμολογοῦμεν (print; Koetschau ὁμολογοῖμεν). ὅσπερ ἐπ' αὐτῷ μόνον ἴσως is taken as ‘which perhaps was all that lay in his power’; it may also mean ‘which perhaps belongs to him alone’. ὑπομονῆς: the print omits Koetschau’s ἡμῶν. εἰ τοῦθ' ὃ δὴ πάντα ἄνθρωπον (print): the clause has no verb with δή; Pass B follows the sense Koetschau’s δεῖ requires (‘what every person must’, with γενέσθαι depending on it), and the reading is doubtful. προσήγορον (print, σ faint; Koetschau προήγορον, ‘spokesman’) is doubtful; rendered ‘on familiar terms with Him’ (LSJ προσήγορος: addressing, affable, familiar; the facing Latin has familiaris). Reviewer re-read PDF p.93 col. A at 300 dpi: the print reads ὃ δὴ and προσηγό-ρον across the line break. ‘Friend of God’ may echo James 2:23 or Wisdom 7:27, ‘beginning and end’ of piety may recall Proverbs 1:7, and ‘abide in Him’ may recall 1 John 2:6, 2:28; ‘made like Him by a pure mind’ is closer to the Platonic likeness to God (Theaetetus 176b) and Matthew 5:8 is at most a distant echo. None is a clear quotation or allusion, so none is cited inline. ‘Golden face of justice’ may echo a line of Euripides quoted by Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics 5.1, 1129b); not Scripture. Pronouns for God are capitalized (‘Him’) to follow the house rule for divine names; adjust if the site style uses lowercase.
